questions.title: Site of protraction and retraction
questions.question: Which of the following is a site for protraction and retraction movements?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The elbow is a hinge joint permitting flexion and extension, not the protraction/retraction pair.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The foot is the site of inversion and eversion (tested separately in this same exam), not protraction/retraction.
explanations.C: Correct. Protraction and retraction are temporomandibular-joint movements: protraction glides the mandible forward, retraction pulls it back. These movements let the lower jaw slide horizontally beneath the upper jaw, distinct from the joint's separate opening/closing (depression/elevation) movements. Loss of smooth protraction/retraction is a recognised finding in temporomandibular joint dysfunction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thumb's characteristic movement is opposition, not protraction/retraction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mandible/temporomandibular joint as the site of protraction and retraction.

questions.title: Origin of the epiphysis
questions.question: The epiphysis of a bone develops from which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Periosteum covers the shaft's external surface and contributes to appositional bone growth, not to the epiphysis's own ossification.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The primary ossification center forms the diaphysis (shaft), not the epiphysis.
explanations.C: Correct. Secondary ossification centres appear in the cartilaginous epiphyses after birth and form each epiphysis. As they expand they leave behind an epiphyseal plate of growth cartilage between epiphysis and metaphysis. Articular cartilage covering the joint surface is the one cartilage in this region never replaced by bone, even into adulthood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Upper epiphyseal plate of cartilage" names a structure (the growth plate itself), not the ossification centre that gives rise to the epiphysis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the epiphysis develops from a secondary ossification centre.

questions.title: Meaning of "lateral"
questions.question: Which of the following is correct concerning the meaning of "Lateral"?

options.B: Near and parallel to the median plane
options.C: Near the back of the body

explanations.A: Correct. Medial and lateral are measured from the median plane: lateral means away from it, toward the side of the body; medial means toward it. Proximal and distal, by contrast, are measured from the root of a limb -- a different reference axis entirely.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Near and parallel to the median plane" describes medial, the opposite of lateral.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Near the back of the body" describes posterior, an entirely different anatomical axis from medial-lateral.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Near front of body" describes anterior, again a different axis from medial-lateral.

questions.learning_objective: State that lateral means away from the median plane.

questions.title: Naming a muscle by its tendon-fibre arrangement
questions.question: Which of the following is the term for a muscle in which the tendon receives muscle fibres from one side?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A bipennate muscle's tendon receives fibres from both sides of a central tendon, not one side only.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A multipennate muscle's tendon receives fibres from several directions onto a branching tendon, not one side only.
explanations.C: Correct. Pennate muscles are classed by how their fascicles meet the tendon. A unipennate muscle's fascicles approach the tendon from one side only, at an angle, resembling one side of a feather. This one-sided arrangement packs more fibres into a given muscle volume than a parallel-fibred muscle, at some cost to the total range of shortening.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Circumpinnate" is not a recognised pennate-muscle classification; it is a distractor term, not a real category.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a muscle as unipennate from its fascicles approaching the tendon from one side only.

questions.title: Territory drained by the right lymphatic duct
questions.question: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from which of the following parts?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The abdomen drains via the thoracic duct (through the cisterna chyli), not the right lymphatic duct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left lower limb drains via the thoracic duct, the larger of the two terminal lymph ducts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left upper limb also drains via the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct.
explanations.D: Correct. The right lymphatic duct drains one quadrant of the body -- the right side of the head, neck, thorax and right upper limb. The thoracic duct, the larger of the two terminal lymph ducts, drains the other three quadrants. The right lymphatic duct empties into the venous system at the right venous angle, near the junction of the right subclavian and internal jugular veins.

questions.learning_objective: State that the right lymphatic duct drains the right quadrant of the body, while the thoracic duct drains the rest.

questions.title: Lining structure damaged in celiac disease
questions.question: In celiac disease (gluten sensitivity), there is malabsorption. Which part of the lining epithelium would you expect to be damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytoplasm as a whole is not the specific structure named in the malabsorption mechanism of celiac disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Organelles in general are not the specific structure damaged; the injury is localised to the absorptive surface.
explanations.C: Correct. Celiac disease is an autoimmune response to dietary gluten that damages the small intestine's absorptive lining. It flattens and destroys the microvilli of the brush border, the apical surface specialisation responsible for most nutrient absorption. Loss of this absorptive surface area is why malabsorption results.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nucleus is not the structure implicated in the malabsorptive mechanism of celiac disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that celiac disease damages the microvilli of the small-intestinal lining, causing malabsorption.

questions.title: Stain for reticular fibres
questions.question: Which of the following is used to stain reticular fibres?

explanations.A: Incorrect. PAS alone stains reticular fibres, but the printed key names the combined technique specifically, not PAS in isolation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Silver stain alone (demonstrating the argyrophilic property) is part of the technique, but not the complete combined answer the key specifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sudan III stains lipids/fat, an entirely unrelated tissue component from the collagenous reticular fibre network.
explanations.D: Correct. Reticular fibres are branching, argyrophilic (silver-staining) and PAS-positive, and invisible on routine H&E staining -- so a silver stain combined with PAS is the technique used to demonstrate them, made by reticular cells that are modified fibroblasts of an organ's supporting stroma. Note this printed key is a plurality only (90/193, 47%), worth a second look.

questions.learning_objective: State that reticular fibres are demonstrated by silver stain (argyrophilia) combined with PAS.

questions.title: Structure damaged by cigarette smoking
questions.question: A biopsy report showed that cigarette smoking caused destruction of the epithelial lining. Which part of the lining epithelium would you expect to be damaged?

explanations.A: Correct. The respiratory tract's pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium relies on its cilia to sweep the mucus blanket, trapped particles and pathogens up and out of the airway. Cigarette smoke damages and destroys these cilia, disabling this mucociliary clearance mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytoplasm as a whole is not the specific apical specialisation named in the smoke-injury mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nuclei are not the structure implicated in the mucociliary-clearance injury caused by smoking.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Microvilli are a small-intestine (and proximal-tubule) surface specialisation for absorption, not a feature of respiratory epithelium — this distractor tests whether a student confuses it with the unrelated celiac-disease question elsewhere in the same exam.

questions.learning_objective: State that cigarette smoke damages the respiratory epithelium's cilia, disabling mucociliary clearance.

questions.title: Cell junction allowing molecular passage
questions.question: Which of the following is the type of cell junction that allows the passage of molecules between adjacent epithelial cells?

explanations.A: Correct. The gap junction is the only one of the four lateral junctions through which anything actually passes: paired channels, each built of six symmetrical transmembrane protein subunits, carry ions, small molecules and (between muscle cells) electrical impulses directly between adjacent cells. It is not part of the junctional complex, which is built from the other three junctions instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The macula adherens (desmosome) is a calcium-dependent anchoring junction that provides mechanical strength; it does not allow molecules to pass between cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The zonula adherens is an adhesion belt anchoring the actin cytoskeleton; it seals cells together rather than permitting molecular passage between them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zonula occludens (tight junction) actually fuses the adjacent membranes to seal the intercellular space, specifically preventing free passage between cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the gap junction as the lateral junction that allows molecules to pass between adjacent cells.

questions.title: What pinocytosis takes into the cell
questions.question: Which of the following can be taken in by the cell membrane through the process of pinocytosis?

explanations.A: Correct. The membrane takes material in by phagocytosis (large solid particles), pinocytosis (fluid) or receptor-mediated endocytosis (specific molecules), and expels material by exocytosis. Pinocytosis, literally "cell drinking", is specifically the fluid-uptake route.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Old organelles are broken down internally (autophagy, forming autolysosomes), not taken in from outside the cell by pinocytosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Solid particles are taken in by phagocytosis, a distinct process from the fluid uptake of pinocytosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Discrete food particles are engulfed by phagocytosis, not pinocytosis, which specifically takes in fluid.

questions.learning_objective: State that pinocytosis takes fluid particles into the cell.

questions.title: Cause of RER basophilia
questions.question: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is basophilic due to the presence of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Acidic protein" is not the specific structure responsible for RER's staining property -- ribosomal RNA is what carries the negative charge that binds basic dyes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysosomes are unrelated organelles, not attached to or responsible for rough ER's basophilia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Protein" alone is too non-specific; it is the ribosome's RNA content, not protein generically, that produces the basophilic staining.
explanations.D: Correct. Free ribosomes make protein the cell keeps for itself, while attached ribosomes, studded on the rough ER's cytoplasmic face, make protein for export. Both are composed largely of ribosomal RNA, whose phosphate backbone carries a strong negative charge. That negative charge is what binds basic dyes such as haematoxylin, producing the basophilic staining of ribosome-rich cytoplasm and rough ER.

questions.learning_objective: State that ribosomes are responsible for the basophilic staining of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
